story.headline: Basel lose 0:3 on Jokanovic debut
story.summary: Basel lost 0:3 at newly promoted Vaduz (a Liechtenstein club playing in the Swiss league) in the first competitive game under new coach Slavisa Jokanovic
story.display_body: Basel lost 0:3 at newly promoted Vaduz (a Liechtenstein club playing in the Swiss league) in the first competitive game under new coach Slavisa Jokanovic. It is Basel's first defeat of the season after 3 wins and 1 draw in their previous games, and it drops them to 7th. Two goals from Marcel Monsberger inside ten minutes settled it. Jokanovic had already called his side "amateurish" after a 3:7 friendly loss to Winterthur during the international break. Earlier the same day, Young Boys won 2:0 at Grasshoppers, only their second clean sheet this season. SRF puts YB six points behind league leaders Lugano, so the title picture is Lugano ahead with the traditional heavyweights unsettled. The league now pauses for the Swiss Cup, with Basel at Stade Nyonnais on 2026-10-16.
story.why: The Swiss title race is unusually open, and the club most expected to challenge, Basel, now has a coaching reset and a crisis of form.

story.headline: Man City win 3:0 at Anfield amid ruling
story.summary: Manchester City beat Liverpool 3:0 (goals from Haaland, Doku and Cherki) in their first game since an independent commission found them guilty of 114 charges of breaching Premier League financial rule
story.display_body: Manchester City beat Liverpool 3:0 (goals from Haaland, Doku and Cherki) in their first game since an independent commission found them guilty of 114 charges of breaching Premier League financial rules between 2009-10 and 2017-18. The win leaves City three points clear at the top. City have appealed, and sanctions, which BBC Sport says have been floated as anything from a record points deduction to relegation, have not been decided. BBC's Phil McNulty argues every result now carries an "asterisk" until the appeal and penalty are settled, and no one knows when that will be. These are the club's contested findings under appeal, not final sanctions.
story.why: If a heavy penalty eventually lands, the table being played out now could be rewritten, which makes the title race provisional.

story.headline: Antonelli nears title after Singapore GP
story.summary: Max Verstappen won in Singapore for the first time at his tenth attempt, 7.3 seconds clear of Charles Leclerc
story.display_body: Max Verstappen won in Singapore for the first time at his tenth attempt, 7.3 seconds clear of Charles Leclerc. The bigger story is the championship: Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli, third, leads team-mate George Russell (ninth after starting 19th) by 102 points, 340 to 238. With 25 points for a win and five rounds left after the United States Grand Prix in Austin, Antonelli can clinch there. The simplest route is to win while Russell finishes ninth or lower; the tie is then broken on race wins (Antonelli has eight to Russell's three). Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton lost a likely podium after staying out during a virtual safety car (a slow-down period under which pit stops are cheap), which Hamilton took the blame for. Standings: Hamilton 229, Verstappen 221, Leclerc 215, Norris 201; points per Autosport's analysis (single outlet).
story.why: The 2026 title is effectively decided, and the open question is the date, with Austin the first chance.

story.headline: FIA admits Singapore qualifying error
story.summary: After a red flag, race control failed to re-enable the cars' overtake mode in time, then briefly switched it back on for 27 seconds before turning it off again
story.display_body: After a red flag, race control failed to re-enable the cars' overtake mode in time, then briefly switched it back on for 27 seconds before turning it off again. Drivers eliminated in that phase of qualifying felt they were hurt unfairly. FIA single-seater director Nikolas Tombazis called it "the worst thing" for the federation and "a bit of a mess, quite frankly", blaming a missed on-screen prompt under time pressure. He said the error affected some drivers more than others.
story.why: It is the sport's governing body admitting that a procedural slip altered a competitive result.

story.headline: Zheng wins China Open as wildcard
story.summary: Zheng Qinwen, a wildcard (an invited entry) ranked 54th, beat fourth seed Mirra Andreeva 7-5 6-4 to become the first Chinese woman to win the event
story.display_body: Zheng Qinwen, a wildcard (an invited entry) ranked 54th, beat fourth seed Mirra Andreeva 7-5 6-4 to become the first Chinese woman to win the event. It is her first WTA 1000 title (the tour's top tier below the Grand Slams) and ends a two-year title drought after elbow surgery last year; she climbs 31 places in the rankings.
story.why: A comeback from injury at home, and a swing in the rankings ahead of the season's final stretch.

story.headline: Riyadh airport struck again
story.summary: A projectile struck King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh on the evening of Sunday 11 October, killing a Pakistani resident and injuring 11, Saudi Arabia's civil aviation authority said, a day after the deadliest strike on the airport so far.
story.display_body: A projectile struck King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh on the evening of Sunday 11 October, killing a Pakistani resident and injuring 11, Saudi Arabia's civil aviation authority said, a day after the deadliest strike on the airport so far. A witness on a taxiing plane told Reuters it hit the tarmac next to parked aircraft at about 20:30 local time and started a fire, and Al Jazeera says the strike was on terminals 3 and 4, which serve domestic flights. India's embassy said one of its citizens died of injuries from Saturday's attack, which raises that toll to 13. Al Jazeera counts four strikes on the airport in five days, and the airport has been closed since Saturday. The Houthis claimed the earlier strikes, but Al Jazeera reports no claim yet for Sunday's. UN Secretary-General António Guterres said late on Saturday that attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure violate international law and "must cease immediately". On Monday 12 October Australia and New Zealand joined the US, Canada, the UK, South Korea and Japan in warning their citizens against travel to the kingdom.
story.why: Gulf aviation is now a regular target, and Western governments are telling their citizens to stay away. That makes it more likely that the US joins the war in Yemen, which President Trump says he is weighing.

story.headline: Trump claims Russia-Ukraine energy truce
story.summary: US President Donald Trump announced on Sunday 11 October that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an immediate "energy ceasefire", but neither Moscow nor Kyiv had confirmed any such deal, and Russian strikes on Ukrainian power infrastructure continued.
story.display_body: US President Donald Trump announced on Sunday 11 October that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an immediate "energy ceasefire", but neither Moscow nor Kyiv had confirmed any such deal, and Russian strikes on Ukrainian power infrastructure continued. "Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE… Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!", Trump wrote on Truth Social, without giving any details. Volodymyr Zelensky told Axios within minutes that the announcement was "news for me". He said Ukraine would accept a halt if Russia did, and asked Washington to say when it starts. Later the same day he said a drone had hit a Kyiv power plant and caused blackouts in the capital. Moscow has not commented. The claim follows Trump's deal on Friday 9 October to buy Russian diesel to lower fuel prices before the US midterms. DW notes that the deal undercuts US sanctions on Russian energy that Trump signed only weeks ago. Zelensky first offered a mutual halt to energy strikes in September.
story.why: the claim has no confirmation from either side, and Trump has spent the week pressing Kyiv to stop hitting Russian refineries. It reads as a demand on Ukraine more than an agreement, until Moscow confirms it and the strikes stop.

story.headline: Slovenes reject Janša inquiry-law change
story.summary: Slovenian voters narrowly rejected the Janez Janša government's amendment to the Parliamentary Inquiry Act in a binding referendum on Sunday 11 October: 51.3% against and 48.7% for, with 99.97% of votes counted, according to the State Election Commission.
story.display_body: Slovenian voters narrowly rejected the Janez Janša government's amendment to the Parliamentary Inquiry Act in a binding referendum on Sunday 11 October: 51.3% against and 48.7% for, with 99.97% of votes counted, according to the State Election Commission. The count stands at 471,859 against and 448,643 for, on a turnout of 54.6% of about 1.7 million voters. The amendment would have obliged people summoned by parliamentary commissions of inquiry to appear at once, without first being able to challenge the summons in court before the commission finished its work. The opposition called this a "political police". Three consultative questions were on the same ballot, on social assistance, voting rights for foreigners and the RTV licence fee. The licence-fee question was decided by fewer than 700 votes. Janša returned to power after the liberal former prime minister Robert Golob failed to form a government, even though Golob's party narrowly won the March election.
story.why: it is the first national vote against the new government's programme, which includes cutting public-sector jobs and funding for civil-rights NGOs. The opposition presented the vote as a test of Slovenia's democratic resilience.

story.headline: Air strikes kill gold miners near Halayeb
story.summary: At least 72 artisanal gold miners were killed in air strikes on Saturday 10 October in the disputed Halayeb border area between Sudan and Egypt, the Sudan-based rights group Emergency Lawyers said on Sunday 11 October, accusing the Egyptian air force.
story.display_body: At least 72 artisanal gold miners were killed in air strikes on Saturday 10 October in the disputed Halayeb border area between Sudan and Egypt, the Sudan-based rights group Emergency Lawyers said on Sunday 11 October, accusing the Egyptian air force. The strikes hit rugged ground south of the Halayeb triangle, east of the Nile, which both Cairo and Khartoum claim and which is known for illegal gold mining and smuggling. Egypt has not commented. It has previously acknowledged a "large-scale operation" against illegal mining inside its borders, after similar strikes on mining sites in the same area in June. The remote location makes independent verification hard, and a witness quoted by DW said nobody knows exactly how many died. Chatham House estimates that up to 60% of Sudan's unofficial gold exports end up in Egypt, and that trade helps fund the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), the paramilitary fighting Sudan's army.
story.why: if the attribution holds, Egypt, which backs Sudan's army, is using lethal force against the cross-border gold trade that helps finance the war.

story.headline: Bärbel Bas quits German cabinet and SPD lead
story.summary: German Labour Minister Bärbel Bas resigned on Monday 12 October as both minister and co-leader of the Social Democrats (SPD).
story.display_body: German Labour Minister Bärbel Bas resigned on Monday 12 October as both minister and co-leader of the Social Democrats (SPD). She cited the death of her stepdaughter and public attacks "also from the ranks of the coalition partner", Chancellor Friedrich Merz's CDU/CSU. "As I currently cannot muster the strength to fully carry out my government and party work at short notice, I have decided to give up both offices," she wrote in a letter circulated by the SPD leadership. SRF's foreign-desk head called the statement a sharp accusation against the chancellor. The CDU had accused her of stalling pension and labour-law reforms. The SPD now needs a new labour minister and a new co-leader alongside Lars Klingbeil.
story.why: losing one of the SPD's two leaders over open coalition friction weakens Merz's government just as it tries to push through pension reform.

story.headline: North Korea fires two ballistic missiles
story.summary: North Korea fired at least two ballistic missiles into the Sea of Japan on the morning of Monday 12 October, one of which flew more than 900 km, according to the South Korean and Japanese militaries.
story.display_body: North Korea fired at least two ballistic missiles into the Sea of Japan on the morning of Monday 12 October, one of which flew more than 900 km, according to the South Korean and Japanese militaries. Japan's Defence Ministry said the first missile, launched at about 09:19 local time, flew about 220 km to a peak altitude of 20 km. The second, launched at 09:36, flew more than 910 km at a peak of 70 km. Both landed outside Japan's exclusive economic zone. Deputy Defence Minister Takashi Koyari said the second missile followed an "irregular" path, which suggests a possible hypersonic weapon (one that can manoeuvre at more than five times the speed of sound, which makes it harder to intercept). The launch came after a South Korean hypersonic test, and after a single ballistic launch by Pyongyang on 3 October.

story.headline: Maillard motion targets premium rises
story.summary: Pierre-Yves Maillard, a Socialist member of the Council of States, wants any average rise in mandatory health-insurance premiums above 3% to need approval by Parliament and be open to an optional referendum. The Federal Council recommended rejecting his motion on 9 September.
story.display_body: Pierre-Yves Maillard, a Socialist member of the Council of States, wants any average rise in mandatory health-insurance premiums above 3% to need approval by Parliament and be open to an optional referendum. The Federal Council recommended rejecting his motion on 9 September. Motion 26.3740 was filed on 18 June. It would require both chambers to ratify the new premiums each autumn session when the average rise exceeds 3%. If a referendum is called, premiums would be frozen until the vote. If voters say no, the government could raise them only in line with consumer prices, and by less than 3%. The average rise of about 5% announced for 2027 would already have crossed that threshold, RTS notes. In its reply the Federal Council says premiums track costs, so the mechanism "would have no effect" on the growth of health spending while seriously disrupting the insurance system. Centrist national councillor Benjamin Roduit argues that voters who reject a rise would also have to say which benefits to cut, which risks a deadlock. RTS says the Council of States could debate the motion in December.
story.why: premiums are a large and rising cost for every household in Switzerland. The motion would give voters a direct check on them, but the government says it would treat the symptom rather than the cost growth behind it.

story.headline: Strasbourg takes Vaud ex-spouse tax case
story.summary: The European Court of Human Rights has declared admissible a complaint that Vaud's rules making ex-spouses jointly liable for tax discriminate against women, Le Temps reported on Monday 12 October.
story.display_body: The European Court of Human Rights has declared admissible a complaint that Vaud's rules making ex-spouses jointly liable for tax discriminate against women, Le Temps reported on Monday 12 October. The case was brought by Lausanne lawyer and Green national councillor Raphaël Mahaim. In 2024 he won the climate case in which the Strasbourg court found that Switzerland had violated the rights of the Senior Women for Climate Protection. Only about 10% of applications get past the admissibility stage, the paper notes. Mahaim calls it "a first small victory". If the court finds against Switzerland, the situation of some Vaud women held liable for their former husbands' tax debts could be reviewed, and similar rules in Appenzell and elsewhere in Europe could change.
story.why: a ruling against Switzerland would force a review of who carries a divorced couple's tax debts, which can fall on the ex-wife long after separation.

story.headline: Bern plans auctions for wine imports
story.summary: Economics Minister Guy Parmelin and the Federal Office for Agriculture plan to auction wine import quotas, which would make foreign wine more expensive and favour Swiss producers, SRF reported on Monday 12 October.
story.display_body: Economics Minister Guy Parmelin and the Federal Office for Agriculture plan to auction wine import quotas, which would make foreign wine more expensive and favour Swiss producers, SRF reported on Monday 12 October. An earlier plan to allow imports only for traders who also buy Swiss grapes was rejected in consultation in the spring. Under the new plan, importers would bid for tariff quotas, and the highest bidders would get them. The office's deputy director, Jean-Marc Chappuis, said not to expect too much from it, because the real problem is that Swiss people, especially younger ones, are drinking less wine while vineyard area has stayed the same, leading to overproduction. Wine merchant Philipp Schwander called it a "crackpot idea" (Schnapsidee) that was rejected 20 years ago, and said Switzerland exports only 1.4% of its wine, compared with 40–60% for Germany, Italy and Spain. The proposal now goes to consultation.

story.headline: Cassis heads to Armenia and Georgia
story.summary: Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis, who chairs the OSCE this year, will visit Armenia and Georgia from Wednesday 14 to Friday 16 October, the Federal Department of Foreign Affairs said on Monday 12 October.
story.display_body: Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis, who chairs the OSCE this year, will visit Armenia and Georgia from Wednesday 14 to Friday 16 October, the Federal Department of Foreign Affairs said on Monday 12 October. In Yerevan on Thursday 15 October he meets Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan and Foreign Minister Ararat Mirzoyan to discuss the Armenia–Azerbaijan peace process. Switzerland says it is ready to offer its expertise if both sides want it. In Tbilisi on Friday 16 October he meets Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze and Foreign Minister Maka Botchorishvili about the consequences of the 2008 war. There Switzerland also holds a protecting-power mandate, acting as diplomatic go-between for Georgia and Russia. The OSCE co-chairs the Geneva International Discussions on the conflict with the UN and the EU.
